Representative examples include BDD-X [[118](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib118)], which extends BDD100K with time-aligned human rationales, where annotators describe why the driver performed a specific action. This dataset provides early grounding for language-based explanations. DriveLM [[225](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib225)] constructs graph-structured question-answer pairs based on nuScenes and CARLA scenarios. These QA pairs target conditional reasoning, enabling models to infer high-level intent, spatial relations, and driving decisions. Impromptu VLA [[36](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib36)] aggregates data from eight public driving datasets and supplements them with captions, instructions, and QA pairs aligned with expert trajectories. The focus is on corner cases and long-tailed events. Other datasets, such as LingoQA [[186](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib186)] and CoVLA [[3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib3)], collect real-world driving videos paired with natural language QA or behavior descriptions, emphasizing spatiotemporal reasoning and human-understandable driving motivations.

Notably, QA-style annotations have emerged as a dominant paradigm for extending driving datasets, serving as a common foundation for training and evaluating reasoning and planning capabilities [[225](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib225), [86](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib86)]. However, the scope and assumptions embedded in such annotations naturally influence model behavior, motivating further exploration of more diverse perspectives, planning horizons, and evaluation protocols for real-world deployment.

Evaluation metrics differ according to the model’s output modality: trajectory-based metrics for continuous action prediction and text-based metrics for models producing linguistic commands or rationales.
Trajectory-based outputs are typically evaluated in open-loop and closed-loop settings.

Open-Loop Evaluation. The predicted trajectory is directly compared against expert trajectories without executing in a simulator. Metrics such as L2 error and collision rate [[91](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib91)], along with trajectory-based indicators including Average Displacement Error (ADE), Final Displacement Error (FDE), and Miss Rate (MR) [[93](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib93)], are widely used. These metrics regard human driving demonstrations as the ground truth and formulate planning essentially as an imitation learning task. By measuring the deviation between predicted and expert trajectories, they provide a straightforward way to assess the accuracy of motion prediction.

Closed-Loop Evaluation. Instead, it measures the model’s performance when interacting with a simulation environment (*e.g.*, CARLA [[56](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib56)]). Representative metrics include route completion (RC), driving score (DS), and infraction distance (ID). Bench2Drive [[103](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib103)] further considers success rate, efficiency, and comfort. NAVSIM [[47](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib47)], built on nuPlan [[18](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib18)], introduces the Predictive Driver Model Score (PDMS), which aggregates subscores for ego progress (EP), time-to-collision (TTC), and comfort (C), while applying penalties on collisions (NC) and driving admissibility (DAC). These metrics provide a holistic view of the safety, feasibility, and deployability of planning actions.

For low-level vehicle control expressed in natural language, evaluation covers both linguistic quality and control effectiveness. Standard text metrics, such as BLEU, ROUGE, and CIDEr, are commonly used to assess the quality of generated language [[328](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib328), [225](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib225)], which measures n-gram overlap with human-annotated reference commands. Beyond command accuracy, reasoning quality is assessed through rationale consistency [[192](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib192)] and human preference ratings of language explanations, particularly in datasets following the BDD-X [[118](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib118)] format. To assess driving applications, execution-based metrics are introduced for behavior assessment. SimLingo [[213](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib213)] introduces an action-dreaming benchmark. The corresponding actions are mapped from the input instruction, which is open-loop evaluated using the success rate.
Regardless of output modality, these benchmarks emphasize key aspects of action quality, including accuracy, executability, safety, and intention alignment.

This section reviews quantitative benchmarks for evaluating VLA models across action prediction, planning accuracy, and closed-loop driving performance. Among them, nuScenes [[17](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib17)], NAVSIM [[47](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib47)], and Bench2Drive [[103](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib103)] are the most widely used. More recently, WOD-E2E [[283](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib283)] introduces long-tail, safety-critical scenes with human-preference annotations, enabling more robust assessment of modern E2E and VLA systems.

The nuScenes open-loop benchmark evaluates planning quality using trajectory-based metrics, including L2 displacement error and Collision Rate, as summarized in Table [5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#S5.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 5.1.2 Vision-Language-Action Datasets ‣ 5.1 Datasets for VLA in Autonomous Driving ‣ 5 Datasets & Benchmark ‣ Vision-Language-Action Models for Autonomous Driving: Past, Present, and Future"). Basically, vision-action models such as UniAD [[93](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib93)] reports 0.69m L2 and 0.12 collision rate. Incorporating language generally improves performance by providing semantic cues for safer planning. For instance, Drive-R1 [[147](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib147)] combines supervised CoT alignment with RL finetuning to reach 0.31m L2 and 0.09 collision rate.

Beyond accuracy, recent studies explore the role of language in handling complex and long-tailed driving scenarios. While improvements are most evident in common cases, rare and highly complex situations remain an active area of investigation, motivating the integration of richer reasoning signals and data sources.

From a systems perspective, computational efficiency is an important consideration for practical deployment. Lightweight and efficiency-oriented designs, such as InsightDrive [[227](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib227)] (16.3 FPS) and token-pruned architectures like FastDriveVLA [[19](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib19)], illustrate ongoing efforts to balance model capacity with real-time feasibility. For cross-domain evaluation, nuScenes highlights generalization to unseen cities and distribution shifts as a key benchmark dimension. Works such as VLP [[197](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib197)] and DiMA [[88](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib88)] examine this setting and motivate complementary strategies including domain adaptation, distillation, and data augmentation.

The Waymo Open Dataset for End-to-End Driving (WOD-E2E) [[283](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib283)] is a large-scale benchmark designed to evaluate end-to-end driving systems under long-tail, safety-critical scenarios that rarely appear in conventional datasets. It contains 4K segments with high-level routing commands, ego-status signals, and multi-camera views, enabling rigorous assessment of perception-planning coupling. A key contribution of WOD-E2E is the Rater Feedback Score (RFS), which measures trajectory quality based on alignment with human preference annotations rather than logged expert trajectories. As shown in Table [6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#S5.T6 "Table 6 ‣ 5.2.2 Text-Based Action Evaluation ‣ 5.2 Evaluation Metrics ‣ 5 Datasets & Benchmark ‣ Vision-Language-Action Models for Autonomous Driving: Past, Present, and Future"), RFS (Overall and Spotlight) complements conventional ADE metrics by providing a more human-aligned assessment of driving behavior.

Overall results indicate that while vision–action models achieve stable displacement accuracy, VLA models exhibit more diverse performance. Approaches such as Poutine [[216](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib216)], and dVLM-AD [[179](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib179)] achieve balanced RFS and ADE performance, highlighting the importance of effectively aligning language reasoning with trajectory generation. Figure [7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#S6.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ 6.1.1 Model Architecture and System Efficiency ‣ 6.1 Current Challenges ‣ 6 Challenges & Future Directions ‣ Vision-Language-Action Models for Autonomous Driving: Past, Present, and Future") presents the visualized performance of AutoVLA [[340](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib340)] in the WOD-E2E dataset.

NAVSIM [[47](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib47)] is built on OpenScene (a redistribution of nuPlan [[18](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib18)]), provides a closed-loop simulation environment designed to evaluate planning quality under realistic urban driving conditions. It adopts the PDMS metric, which aggregates multiple driving aspects, including No-Collision (NC), Driving Admissibility (DAC), Time-to-Collision (TTC), Ego Progress (EP), and Comfort (C), offering a holistic assessment of safety, efficiency, and driving smoothness. As shown in Table [7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#S5.T7 "Table 7 ‣ 5.2.2 Text-Based Action Evaluation ‣ 5.2 Evaluation Metrics ‣ 5 Datasets & Benchmark ‣ Vision-Language-Action Models for Autonomous Driving: Past, Present, and Future"), most methods achieve strong performance on safety-related metrics such as NC and DAC, while TTC and EP serve as more discriminative indicators of planning foresight and long-horizon decision quality. These metrics highlight differences in how models balance safety and progress when interacting with dynamic environments.

Representative vision–action approaches, such as WoTE [[145](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib145)], achieve 88.3 PDMS by integrating a BEV-based world model with reward-guided trajectory selection, demonstrating the effectiveness of structured world modeling for closed-loop planning. Building upon this foundation, language-conditioned methods further enhance decision-making. For instance, AutoVLA [[340](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib340)] improves performance to 99.1 NC and 87.6 EP by leveraging language-driven decision priors and a Best-of-N oracle scoring strategy, illustrating how language supervision can guide trajectory selection and improve long-horizon planning behavior.

Bench2Drive [[103](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib103)] provides a closed-loop evaluation protocol built on CARLA V2, focusing on success rate and composite driving scores to assess goal-directed driving behavior under interactive settings. Unlike open-loop benchmarks, Bench2Drive explicitly evaluates an agent’s ability to execute long-horizon tasks and respond to dynamic environmental feedback.

Recent VLA approaches demonstrate clear benefits from language grounding in this benchmark. For example, SimLingo [[213](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib213)] introduces an action dreaming mechanism that aligns natural language instructions with control sequences, achieving a leading driving score of 85.94, as reported in Table [8](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#S5.T8 "Table 8 ‣ 5.2.2 Text-Based Action Evaluation ‣ 5.2 Evaluation Metrics ‣ 5 Datasets & Benchmark ‣ Vision-Language-Action Models for Autonomous Driving: Past, Present, and Future"). These results indicate that language-guided reasoning can effectively influence closed-loop decision-making and improve planning performance in interactive driving scenarios.

Taken together with open-loop benchmarks, Bench2Drive highlights the growing importance of language–action alignment in VLA systems, particularly for interpreting high-level goals, guiding long-horizon behavior, and adapting actions under complex, human-centered instructions.

VLA models mark a shift from modular stacks toward holistic, reasoning-driven driving agents. By leveraging large multimodal backbones, they promise richer environmental understanding, stronger generalization, and more interpretable decision-making. Yet, realizing their full potential in safety-critical autonomous driving requires addressing several fundamental challenges. In parallel, emerging research directions point toward next-generation systems that are more efficient, trustworthy, and capable of long-horizon reasoning.

Real-Time Processing and Latency. VLA models inherit the substantial computational footprint of modern vision-language backbones. High-resolution, high-frame-rate camera inputs generate long visual-token sequences, and multi-view fusion amplifies memory and latency costs. Meeting the strict real-time constraints of autonomous vehicles, therefore, remains difficult [[111](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib111), [269](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib269)]. Recent advances in streaming token compression and adaptive visual encoders [[139](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib139), [19](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib19)] offer promising directions, but achieving sub-50ms inference remains an unmet requirement for safety-critical deployment.

Lack of Domain-Specific Foundation Models. General-purpose VLMs [[6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib6), [35](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib35), [343](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib343)] provide strong priors but are not optimized for driving-specific perception, physics, or multi-sensor fusion. Autonomous driving requires precise spatial reasoning, adherence to traffic rules, and an understanding of rare, high-stakes edge cases – abilities not fully captured by generic models. As highlighted in Section [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#S3 "3 Vision-Action Models ‣ Vision-Language-Action Models for Autonomous Driving: Past, Present, and Future"), dedicated driving foundation models [[152](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib152)] remain a missing cornerstone for scalable and dependable VLA systems.

Generalizing to Rare and Novel Scenarios. One motivation for VLAs is their ability to leverage strong visual-language priors to interpret complex scenes. However, while VLM components may generalize well perceptually, aligning this understanding to the action space introduces new uncertainties. As noted in Section [4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#S4 "4 Vision-Language-Action Models ‣ Vision-Language-Action Models for Autonomous Driving: Past, Present, and Future"), reasoning-rich representations do not automatically translate to robust action generation. Long-tailed scenarios – misbehaving traffic agents, unusual road layouts, unpredictable weather – remain failure points [[74](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib74), [302](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib302), [311](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib311), [247](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib247), [48](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib48)].

Cost of High-Quality Data. VLAs rely on diverse, high-quality multimodal datasets [[163](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib163), [132](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib132)], yet collecting paired vision-action-language triplets at scale is expensive. Synthetic environments [[228](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib228), [22](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib22), [191](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib191)] help, but face substantial sim-to-real gaps, with discrepancies in noise characteristics, lighting, and behavior of other agents [[123](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib123), [274](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib274)]. Improving data efficiency and mitigating distribution shifts remain long-standing challenges.

Interpretability & Hallucination. While VLA models produce natural-language rationales via chain-of-thought prompting [[67](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib67), [340](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib340), [261](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib261)], these explanations are generated artifacts – not faithful reflections of the underlying causal reasoning. Language hallucination [[211](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib211), [159](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib159), [94](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib94)] presents new risks: the model may justify an incorrect decision with a confident but spurious narrative. Ensuring consistent grounding between perceptions, actions, and explanations is an open challenge.

Long-Horizon Temporal Coherence. Driving depends on anticipating multi-stage interactions and maintaining situational awareness across extended time horizons [[199](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib199), [229](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib229), [285](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib285)]. Current transformer-based VLA architectures remain constrained by limited context windows and short-term conditioning, inherited from standard VLM designs. Temporal fragmentation leads to inconsistent decisions, especially in multi-agent or highly dynamic traffic scenes.

Unified Vision-Language-World Models. A promising evolution integrates VLA with predictive world models [[9](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib9), [21](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib21), [144](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib144), [143](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib143)], extending the VA-based models in Section [3.2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#S3.SS2 "3.2 World Models for Autonomous Driving ‣ 3 Vision-Action Models ‣ Vision-Language-Action Models for Autonomous Driving: Past, Present, and Future"). Rather than reacting frame by frame, such systems simulate future scene evolution conditioned on candidate actions, enabling proactive planning and more reliable behavior under uncertainty. Building unified, end-to-end world models that jointly reason about perception, language, and dynamics may form the backbone of next-generation autonomous agents.

Richer Multimodal Fusion. As sensor suites diversify, future architectures will incorporate early and tight fusion of LiDAR, Radar, event cameras, and high-definition maps [[123](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib123), [274](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib274), [222](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib222)]. Language enhances semantic grounding, but robust 3D geometry is indispensable for safe decision-making [[167](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib167), [248](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib248)]. Holistic multimodal fusion can combine the interpretability of VLMs with the spatial precision of geometric sensors.

Socially Aware, Knowledge-Grounded Driving. VLA models must acquire deeper commonsense reasoning – understanding intent, conventions, and causal relationships beyond explicit annotations [[140](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib140), [313](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib313)]. Future efforts will draw from large-scale video-language corpora, leveraging external knowledge bases and structured reasoning modules to support socially compliant and anticipatory driving.

Continual & Onboard Learning. Static, offline-trained models cannot capture evolving road infrastructures or regional driving customs [[255](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib255), [344](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib344), [20](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib20)]. Enabling safe, incremental learning from everyday driving, while avoiding catastrophic forgetting and ensuring safety guarantees, is essential for long-term deployment. This relates closely to addressing long-tail generalization gaps.

Standardized Evaluation & Safety Guarantees. Evaluation metrics from current benchmarks, *e.g.*, NAVSIM [[47](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib47)] and Bench2Drive [[103](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib103)], assess safety and comfort but do not capture key VLA-specific risks such as reasoning failures, instruction-following errors, or cross-modal inconsistencies [[159](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib159), [211](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib211)]. Future benchmarks should evaluate multi-step instruction execution, robustness to ambiguous language, and resistance to hallucination. Beyond empirical testing, formal verification tools are needed to provide theoretical guarantees for safety-critical behaviors.

Human-Centric Interaction & Personalization. VLA systems open the door to richer in-car interaction [[295](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib295), [219](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib219)]. Natural language enables drivers to specify goals, constraints, and preferences (“drive cautiously”, “avoid unprotected left turns”). Personalization modules [[81](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib81)] can adapt driving styles to different users, enhancing comfort and trust. The challenge lies in balancing personalization with strict safety and regulatory requirements.

Vision-Language-Action models are reshaping autonomous driving by coupling perception with high-level reasoning and natural language understanding. This work formalizes the VLA problem setting, outlines the progression from traditional VA pipelines, and organizes existing methods into coherent architectural families together with the datasets and benchmarks that support their development. VLA systems offer clear advantages in interpretability, generalization, and human interaction, but core challenges remain: aligning symbolic reasoning with continuous control, ensuring robustness in long-tail scenarios, and establishing evaluation protocols that faithfully measure instruction following and safety. Progress will depend on advances in efficient architectures, deeper multimodal fusion, world-model-driven planning, and more rigorous human-centered testing. Overall, VLA represents a promising direction for building autonomous agents that are not only competent drivers but also communicative, transparent, and responsive to human intent.

chunks.text: # Vision-Language-Action Models for Autonomous Driving: Past, Present, and Future

heading_path: Vision-Language-Action Models for Autonomous Driving: Past, Present, and Future
chunks.text:
###### Abstract

Autonomous driving has long relied on modular “Perception-Decision-Action” pipelines, where hand-crafted interfaces and rule-based components often break down in complex or long-tailed scenarios. Their cascaded design further propagates perception errors, degrading downstream planning and control. Vision-Action (VA) models address some limitations by learning direct mappings from visual inputs to actions, but they remain opaque, sensitive to distribution shifts, and lack structured reasoning or instruction-following capabilities. Recent progress in Large Language Models (LLMs) and multimodal learning has motivated the emergence of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) frameworks, which integrate perception with language-grounded decision making. By unifying visual understanding, linguistic reasoning, and actionable outputs, VLAs offer a more interpretable, generalizable, and human-aligned paradigm for driving policies. This work provides a structured characterization of the emerging VLA landscape for autonomous driving. We trace the evolution from early VA approaches to modern VLA frameworks and organize existing methods into two principal paradigms: *End-to-End VLA*, which integrates perception, reasoning, and planning within a single model, and *Dual-System VLA*, which separates slow deliberation (via VLMs) from fast, safety-critical execution (via planners). Within these paradigms, we further distinguish subclasses such as textual *vs.* numerical action generators and explicit *vs.* implicit guidance mechanisms. We also summarize representative datasets and benchmarks for evaluating VLA-based driving systems and highlight key challenges and open directions, including robustness, interpretability, and instruction fidelity. Overall, this work aims to establish a coherent foundation for advancing human-compatible autonomous driving systems.

chunks.text:
## 1 Introduction

The pursuit of fully autonomous driving (AD) has long been a central goal in AI and robotics [[73](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib73), [38](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib38), [124](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib124)]. Conventional AD systems typically adopt a modular “Perception-Decision-Action” pipeline, where mapping [[82](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib82), [83](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib83)], object detection [[150](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib150), [199](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib199), [123](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib123), [153](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib153)], motion prediction [[307](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib307), [117](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib117), [55](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib55)], and trajectory planning [[151](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib151), [308](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib308)] are developed and optimized as separate components. While this design has achieved strong performance in structured environments, its reliance on hand-crafted interfaces and rules limits adaptability in complex [[84](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib84), [85](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib85), [220](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib220)], dynamic [[274](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib274), [275](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib275), [122](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib122)], and long-tailed scenarios [[197](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib197), [74](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib74), [302](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib302)]. Moreover, the sequential cascade is prone to cross-stage error propagation, where perception noise is amplified by downstream reasoning and control, compromising stability and safety.

To mitigate these issues, research has increasingly moved toward end-to-end autonomous driving, where Vision-Action (VA) models directly map raw sensory inputs to control commands or trajectory waypoints using imitation [[43](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib43), [198](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib198), [204](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib204)] and reinforcement learning [[151](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib151), [281](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib281), [68](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib68)]. Early systems such as ALVINN [[203](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib203)] and ChauffeurNet [[10](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib10)] demonstrated the viability of behavior cloning at scale. Subsequent advances introduced more expressive architectures: TransFuser [[40](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib40)] exploited transformer-based multimodal fusion, UniAD [[93](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib93)] unified perception and planning, VAD [[108](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib108)] leveraged vectorized scene representations, DriveTransformer [[104](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib104)] explored scalable transformer backbones, and DiffusionDrive [[156](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib156)] applied generative modeling to multi-modal trajectory prediction. Collectively, these VA models show that complex driving policies can be learned directly from data, laying the foundation for modern end-to-end AD systems.

Despite these successes, VA models exhibit fundamental limitations. They largely behave as “black boxes”, offering limited interpretability in safety-critical settings [[28](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib28), [113](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib113), [189](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib189), [309](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib309), [126](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib126), [125](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib125)]. Their generalization remains fragile under rare or long-tail scenarios that are underrepresented in training [[28](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib28), [110](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib110), [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib3), [309](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib309), [69](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib69), [146](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib146)]. By directly mapping perception to low-level actions, they lack chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning and contextual deliberation [[110](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib110), [28](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib28), [70](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib70), [286](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib286)], limiting their ability to resolve ambiguous or multi-stage interactions. Moreover, their focus on visual inputs prevents them from incorporating high-level plans or human instructions in natural language, leaving a gap in human-vehicle interaction [[110](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib110), [197](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib197), [320](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib320), [222](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib222)].

The emergence of Large Language Models (LLMs) and Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) has catalyzed a new paradigm: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models [[2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib2), [217](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib217), [336](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib336)]. VLA models couple a Vision-Language Model (VLM) backbone with an action-prediction head, enabling direct mapping from multimodal inputs (vision + language) to executable driving actions. By jointly modeling perception, language understanding, and decision-making, VLA frameworks aspire to provide human-like reasoning, interpretability, and instruction-following [[340](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib340), [67](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib67), [72](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib72)]. Initial explorations such as DriveMLM [[264](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib264)] and GPT-Driver [[184](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib184)] introduced language modules into driving pipelines for high-level decision understanding, paving the way for more integrated designs. Later systems advanced toward closed-loop and reasoning-centric VLA models: LMDrive [[222](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib222)] achieved language-guided closed-loop driving, DriveLM [[225](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib225)] enabled structured reasoning via visual question answering, and DriveGPT4 [[287](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib287)] provided natural-language rationales for decisions. Recent works further investigate tightly coupled reasoning and control, including AutoVLA [[340](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib340)] with fast/slow thinking and GRPO-based optimization [[224](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib224)], and SimLingo [[213](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib213)], which explicitly studies language-action alignment.

End-to-End VLA models, however, must simultaneously *reason* and *act* in real time, creating challenges for latency and safety. This has led to *Dual-System* VLA designs, where high-level decision making is separated from low-level trajectory execution. DriveVLM [[249](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib249)] generates textual rationales or decisions with a VLM while relying on a classical planner for trajectories. VLP [[197](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib197)] tokenizes waypoints and value maps to produce planning-aware latent actions, and Diff-VLA [[106](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib106)] synthesizes language-guided trajectories refined by rule- or optimization-based controllers. InsightDrive [[227](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib227)] integrates causal language reasoning with MPC, assigning *why* to the VLM and *how* to the planner.

Together, these developments signal a paradigm shift from perception-driven pipelines toward systems that jointly reason, understand, and act. Given the rapid evolution of this field, there is a need to consolidate its conceptual foundations, clarify architectural trends, and provide a structured analysis of emerging directions.

Contributions. This work provides a comprehensive characterization of VLA models for autonomous driving. Specifically:

* • We chart the evolution from precursor VA models (Section [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#S3 "3 Vision-Action Models ‣ Vision-Language-Action Models for Autonomous Driving: Past, Present, and Future")) to modern VLA frameworks (Section [4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#S4 "4 Vision-Language-Action Models ‣ Vision-Language-Action Models for Autonomous Driving: Past, Present, and Future")), providing historical context and clarifying the motivations behind this paradigm shift. * • We propose a taxonomy that categorizes VLA architectures into End-to-End (Section [4.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#S4.SS1 "4.1 End-to-End VLA for Autonomous Driving ‣ 4 Vision-Language-Action Models ‣ Vision-Language-Action Models for Autonomous Driving: Past, Present, and Future")) and Dual-System (Section [4.2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#S4.SS2 "4.2 Dual-System VLA ‣ 4 Vision-Language-Action Models ‣ Vision-Language-Action Models for Autonomous Driving: Past, Present, and Future")) designs, and compare their principles, advantages, and limitations. * • We present an organized synthesis of datasets and evaluation benchmarks relevant to VLA-based driving (Section [5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#S5 "5 Datasets & Benchmark ‣ Vision-Language-Action Models for Autonomous Driving: Past, Present, and Future")), facilitating consistent and meaningful comparisons. * • We identify key challenges in real-world VLA deployment and outline future research directions (Section [6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#S6 "6 Challenges & Future Directions ‣ Vision-Language-Action Models for Autonomous Driving: Past, Present, and Future")) to guide progress toward safer and more reliable autonomous systems.

We chart the evolution from precursor VA models (Section [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#S3 "3 Vision-Action Models ‣ Vision-Language-Action Models for Autonomous Driving: Past, Present, and Future")) to modern VLA frameworks (Section [4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#S4 "4 Vision-Language-Action Models ‣ Vision-Language-Action Models for Autonomous Driving: Past, Present, and Future")), providing historical context and clarifying the motivations behind this paradigm shift.

We propose a taxonomy that categorizes VLA architectures into End-to-End (Section [4.1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#S4.SS1 "4.1 End-to-End VLA for Autonomous Driving ‣ 4 Vision-Language-Action Models ‣ Vision-Language-Action Models for Autonomous Driving: Past, Present, and Future")) and Dual-System (Section [4.2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#S4.SS2 "4.2 Dual-System VLA ‣ 4 Vision-Language-Action Models ‣ Vision-Language-Action Models for Autonomous Driving: Past, Present, and Future")) designs, and compare their principles, advantages, and limitations.

We present an organized synthesis of datasets and evaluation benchmarks relevant to VLA-based driving (Section [5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#S5 "5 Datasets & Benchmark ‣ Vision-Language-Action Models for Autonomous Driving: Past, Present, and Future")), facilitating consistent and meaningful comparisons.

We identify key challenges in real-world VLA deployment and outline future research directions (Section [6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#S6 "6 Challenges & Future Directions ‣ Vision-Language-Action Models for Autonomous Driving: Past, Present, and Future")) to guide progress toward safer and more reliable autonomous systems.

Scope. This work differs from prior studies on VLA models [[2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib2), [217](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib217), [336](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib336), [110](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib110)] through its domain-specific focus, historical framing, and architectural depth. 1Domain-specific focus. Unlike broader analyses that span robotics or embodied AI [[180](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib180), [223](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib223)], our work *focuses exclusively on autonomous driving*, allowing a fine-grained analysis of driving-specific challenges, dataset characteristics, and safety requirements. 2Historical and conceptual continuity. We adopt a “Past-Present-Future” narrative that traces the path from early VA models to modern VLA frameworks, emphasizing the motivations and technical lineage underlying the integration of language grounding into perception and control. 3Fine-grained architectural taxonomy. Unlike prior high-level overviews [[338](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib338), [299](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib299), [45](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib45), [110](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib110)], we propose a hierarchical taxonomy that differentiates End-to-End and Dual-System VLA models and analyzes how they organize perception, reasoning, and control.

Through this combination of domain specificity, historical depth, and structured architectural analysis, we aim to provide a comprehensive and insightful reference for VLA research in autonomous driving.

Organization. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section [2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#S2 "2 Preliminary Foundations ‣ Vision-Language-Action Models for Autonomous Driving: Past, Present, and Future") introduces the preliminary foundations of VLA frameworks. Section [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#S3 "3 Vision-Action Models ‣ Vision-Language-Action Models for Autonomous Driving: Past, Present, and Future") outlines the evolution of VA models. Section [4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#S4 "4 Vision-Language-Action Models ‣ Vision-Language-Action Models for Autonomous Driving: Past, Present, and Future") presents our taxonomy and analysis of VLA architectures. Section [5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#S5 "5 Datasets & Benchmark ‣ Vision-Language-Action Models for Autonomous Driving: Past, Present, and Future") summarizes datasets and benchmarks. Section [6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#S6 "6 Challenges & Future Directions ‣ Vision-Language-Action Models for Autonomous Driving: Past, Present, and Future") discusses remaining challenges and future directions. Section [7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#S7 "7 Conclusion ‣ Vision-Language-Action Models for Autonomous Driving: Past, Present, and Future") concludes this work.

### 2.2 VLM Backbone (FF)

FF

The VLM backbone F​(⋅)F(\cdot) is the core reasoning engine of the system. It is typically a large vision language model [[160](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib160), [258](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib258), [6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib6), [35](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib35), [343](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib343), [9](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib9)]. Its primary role is to fuse the diverse input modalities into a single, powerful latent representation. It consists of a vision encoder (*e.g.*, a Vision Transformer, ViT) [[210](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib210)] to process visual inputs and an LLM decoder that conditions its generation on the visual features. A bridge network [[160](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib160), [35](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib35)] or unified multimodal token modelling mechanism [[258](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib258), [6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib6)] is used to align the vision features with the language embeddings. VLM can directly generate the actions or provide the guidance for another action expert to develop more robust results.

#### 2.2.1 VLM for Direct Action Generation (Single-System)

In this paradigm, the VLM directly emits actions through its language head [[264](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib264), [184](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib184), [225](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib225), [98](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib98)] or a small attached head [[288](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib288), [222](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib222), [213](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib213)]. This fully end-to-end design exploits the VLM’s reasoning capabilities to map from visual/language inputs to executable controls.

heading_path: Vision-Language-Action Models for Autonomous Driving: Past, Present, and Future
chunks.text:
#### 2.2.2 VLM for Guidance Generation (Dual-System)

Alternatively, the VLM functions as a high-level reasoning module that produces intermediate guidance—textual rationales [[249](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib249), [80](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib80), [207](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib207)] or structured latent intents [[197](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib197), [146](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib146)], which a downstream planner converts into low-level actions [[257](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib257)]. This “slow thinking + fast execution” architecture improves interpretability and enables planners to enforce physical feasibility and safety constraints.

### 2.3 Action Prediction Head (HH)

HH

The head H​(⋅)H(\cdot) converts the VLM latent representation into action outputs. Consistent with the taxonomy used in existing literature, we categorize action heads into four types based on their output formulation and generation mechanism: Language Head (LH), Regression (REG), Trajectory Selection (SEL), and Trajectory Generation (GEN).

H​(⋅)H(\cdot)

* • Language Head (LH). This design directly utilizes the VLM’s inherent text-generation capabilities to produce actions in the language space. The head is typically the language modeling head of the VLM, trained to output either free-form textual commands (*e.g.*, *“turn left”*) [[287](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib287)] or a sequence of discretized action tokens [[340](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib340)]. The model autoregressively predicts these tokens, which are subsequently parsed into executable signals. This approach is widely adopted in textual action generators like DriveMLM [[264](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib264)] and DriveGPT4 [[287](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib287)]. * • Regression (REG). This formulation employs a decoder structure followed by a regressor (typically a Multi-Layer Perceptron) to directly predict continuous values. Unlike language heads, it avoids discretization by mapping the latent features aggregated via Transformers or GRUs to specific numerical outputs such as steering angles, throttle/brake values, or trajectory waypoints. Representative methods using this deterministic approach include LMDrive [[222](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib222)] and DriveGPT4-V2 [[288](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib288)]. * • Trajectory Selection (SEL). Instead of directly regressing a single path, this head evaluates a set of candidate trajectories and selects the optimal one based on a learned cost function or scoring mechanism. The model typically generates or samples a diverse set of dynamically feasible trajectories and uses the latent representation to predict the cost or probability for each candidate. This approach, utilized by methods like WoTE [[145](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib145)] and SeerDrive [[315](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib315)], ensures that the final output adheres to kinematic constraints by selecting from pre-defined candidates. * • Trajectory Generation (GEN). This generative formulation synthesizes actions through probabilistic modeling, most notably using diffusion models or variational autoencoder [[156](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib156), [333](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib333), [106](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib106)]. Starting from noise, the head iteratively refines the trajectory sample conditioned on the VLM latent state and optionally language instructions. This allows the model to capture the multi-modality and uncertainty of future distributions. Prominent examples include ORION [[67](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib67)] and DiffVLA [[106](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib106)].

The head is typically the language modeling head of the VLM, trained to output either free-form textual commands (*e.g.*, *“turn left”*) [[287](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib287)] or a sequence of discretized action tokens [[340](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib340)]. The model autoregressively predicts these tokens, which are subsequently parsed into executable signals. This approach is widely adopted in textual action generators like DriveMLM [[264](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib264)] and DriveGPT4 [[287](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib287)].

### 2.4 Action in Driving

In the context of autonomous driving, particularly for models like VLAs, the action space defines the set of possible outputs the model can generate to control the vehicle. The choice of action representation is a fundamental design decision that dictates how the model’s reasoning is translated into physical motion. We outline three primary paradigms for action space representation below.

#### 2.4.1 Discrete Trajectory Representations

This paradigm represents the vehicle’s intended future path as a finite sequence of spatial waypoints [[168](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib168)]. Each waypoint is a spatial coordinate that the vehicle is expected to reach at a specific future time step. This representation allows for explicit geometric path planning and trajectory optimization. The action, 𝐚t\mathbf{a}\_{t}, formulated at the current time tt, is a set of Φ\Phi future waypoints:

This paradigm leverages the natural language capabilities of VLMs to express driving actions through textual descriptions [[19](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib19)]. The action is represented as a sequence of discrete tokens from a predefined vocabulary:

## 3 Vision-Action Models

Vision-Action (VA) models represent one of the earliest and most influential lines of research in autonomous driving. Their core idea is to directly map sensory observations – typically camera inputs – to driving actions, thereby avoiding explicit modular decomposition into perception, prediction, and planning. Enabled by deep neural networks, VA models have been explored through two major training paradigms: 1*imitation learning*, which distills policies from expert demonstrations, and 2*reinforcement learning*, which optimizes behavior through trial-and-error interaction. More recently, *world models* have expanded this paradigm by enabling agents to simulate scene dynamics and reason about action consequences, improving robustness and scalability. Table [1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.1.1 Action-Only Model ‣ 3.1 End-to-End Models for Autonomous Driving ‣ 3 Vision-Action Models ‣ Vision-Language-Action Models for Autonomous Driving: Past, Present, and Future") provides an overview of representative efforts.

From an architectural perspective, VA methodologies for autonomous driving can be broadly grouped into:

* • End-to-End Models, which directly predict control commands or planned trajectories from sensory inputs. * • World Models, which explicitly model action-conditioned future dynamics to support policy learning and decision-making.

chunks.text:
### 3.1 End-to-End Models for Autonomous Driving

End-to-end (E2E) models learn a single neural network that maps raw or intermediate sensor observations to actions or planned trajectories [[28](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib28), [38](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib38), [145](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib145), [16](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib16)]. Unlike modular stacks, which isolate perception, prediction, and planning, E2E approaches implicitly couple these tasks within a unified representation [[235](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib235), [109](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib109), [91](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib91)]. Depending on whether perception supervision is employed, existing methods fall into two main categories: *action-only models* and *perception-action models*, as illustrated in Figure [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#S3.F3.1 "Figure 3 ‣ 3.1.2 Perception-Action Model ‣ 3.1 End-to-End Models for Autonomous Driving ‣ 3 Vision-Action Models ‣ Vision-Language-Action Models for Autonomous Driving: Past, Present, and Future").

chunks.text:
#### 3.1.1 Action-Only Model

Action-only models adopt a streamlined one-stage formulation: sensory inputs are fed directly into a network that outputs low-level actions. These methods primarily differ in whether policies are learned from demonstrations or through exploration.

Imitation Learning (IL), especially behavior cloning [[7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib7)], learns a policy by matching expert actions, as visualized in the IL branch of Figure [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#S3.F3.1 "Figure 3 ‣ 3.1.2 Perception-Action Model ‣ 3.1 End-to-End Models for Autonomous Driving ‣ 3 Vision-Action Models ‣ Vision-Language-Action Models for Autonomous Driving: Past, Present, and Future"). Early works [[203](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib203), [16](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib16), [198](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib198), [43](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib43)] demonstrated that actions can be predicted directly from monocular or multi-view inputs, and subsequent designs refined backbone architectures [[205](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib205), [24](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib24), [40](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib40)]. NEAT [[39](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib39)] highlights behaviorally relevant image regions via intermediate attention maps, while TCP [[273](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib273)] fuses a trajectory branch and control branch for complementary supervision. To better leverage scene geometry, BEV-Planner [[149](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib149)] predicts trajectories from BEV features enriched with ego states. Urban-Driver [[218](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib218)] moves beyond open-loop evaluation by training policies in a differentiable, data-driven simulator.

IL-based methods are simple, efficient, and require no reward engineering; however, they remain sensitive to distribution shift [[215](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib215), [56](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib56), [206](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib206)] and causal confusion [[190](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib190), [49](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib49), [200](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib200)], which can impair reliability in long-tailed or rare-event scenarios.

Reinforcement Learning (RL) optimizes actions through interaction, offering greater flexibility than imitation-based approaches [[237](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib237), [119](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib119)]. Several works address the sample inefficiency of RL by combining it with supervised pretraining: Latent-DRL [[251](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib251)] and Gri [[23](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib23)] pre-train visual encoders using semantic segmentation, while LSD [[194](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib194)] initializes policies via IL before performing RL fine-tuning. Privileged-information distillation has also proven effective: LBC [[25](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib25)], WoR [[26](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib26)], and Roach [[326](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib326)] use simulator-only states to guide sensor-based agents.

Combined with the world model, Think2Drive [[137](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib137)] trains the agent with the Model-Based RL (MBRL) method, paired with a compact latent world model learning the transitions of the environment. Raw2Drive [[301](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib301)] is a dual-stream MBRL approach, where the raw sensor world model is aligned with the privileged world model for camera-based action prediction. In contrast to studies in non-photorealistic CARLA [[56](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib56)], recent efforts have shifted toward photorealistic world modeling. RAD [[68](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib68)] establishes a 3DGS-based [[116](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib116)] closed-loop RL training paradigm regulated by IL in a realistic 3DGS environment. The key challenges in RL-based models include sample inefficiency [[151](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib151)], reward function design [[120](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib120)], and sim-to-real transfer [[38](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib38)].

heading_path: Vision-Language-Action Models for Autonomous Driving: Past, Present, and Future
chunks.text:
#### 3.1.2 Perception-Action Model

Perception-action models follow a two-stage paradigm in which perception tasks (*e.g.*, mapping, tracking) supervise and constrain trajectory prediction. These methods generally adopt either dense BEV-based representations or sparse query-based representations, as shown in Figure [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#S3.F3.1 "Figure 3 ‣ 3.1.2 Perception-Action Model ‣ 3.1 End-to-End Models for Autonomous Driving ‣ 3 Vision-Action Models ‣ Vision-Language-Action Models for Autonomous Driving: Past, Present, and Future").

Dense BEV-Based Models construct unified top-down features from multi-view cameras. ST-P3 [[91](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib91)] jointly learns spatial-temporal features for perception and planning; UniAD [[93](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib93)] integrates sequential task dependencies to support goal-directed planning. VAD [[108](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib108)] employs a vectorized scene representation to improve both planning safety and efficiency. OccNet [[250](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib250)] incorporates occupancy embeddings to capture 3D scene geometry. Para-Drive [[269](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib269)] proposes a fully parallel E2E architecture for real-time deployment.

Generative and sampling-based approaches have recently emerged: GenAD [[333](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib333)] frames planning as sampling from learned distributions; DiffusionDrive [[156](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib156)] introduces a truncated diffusion policy guided by multi-modal anchors; GuideFlow [[162](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib162)] incorporates explicit physical constraints into the generation process. While BEV representations naturally align with 2D trajectory planning, they require substantial computation due to their dense spatial structure.

Sparse Query-Based Models avoid explicit BEV grids by using latent queries to aggregate image features. SparseAD [[317](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib317)] and SparseDrive [[235](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib235)] represent the entire scene using sparse perception queries and a parallel planner, achieving strong efficiency-accuracy trade-offs. DiFSD [[231](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib231)] introduces an ego-centric sparse formulation and models uncertainty through trajectory denoising. DriveTransformer [[104](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib104)] incorporates task parallelism, sparse attention, and streaming updates for improved stability. GaussianAD [[332](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib332)] adopts 3D semantic Gaussians for fine-grained yet compact scene representation.

Sparse query methods significantly reduce inference latency, but the absence of a dense future-world representation can restrict long-horizon reasoning and planning safety.

heading_path: Vision-Language-Action Models for Autonomous Driving: Past, Present, and Future
chunks.text:
### 3.2 World Models for Autonomous Driving

World models aim to predict how driving scenes evolve under different ego actions [[77](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib77), [291](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib291), [121](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib121)]. By jointly modeling scene dynamics and ego motion, they provide a powerful mechanism for learning safe, long-horizon driving policies [[53](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib53)]. Their applications span immersive simulation [[90](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib90), [175](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib175), [212](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib212), [290](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib290), [13](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib13), [342](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib342)], end-to-end planning [[265](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib265), [69](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib69), [267](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib267), [92](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib92)], and feature learning for downstream tasks [[188](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib188), [298](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib298), [319](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib319), [170](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib170), [29](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib29), [30](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib30), [138](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib138)]. Here, we focus on world models designed for trajectory planning and categorize them by prediction modality and representation granularity into three groups: image-based, occupancy-based, and latent-based models (Figure [4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#S3.F4.1 "Figure 4 ‣ 3.2.1 Image-Based World Model ‣ 3.2 World Models for Autonomous Driving ‣ 3 Vision-Action Models ‣ Vision-Language-Action Models for Autonomous Driving: Past, Present, and Future")).

heading_path: Vision-Language-Action Models for Autonomous Driving: Past, Present, and Future
chunks.text:
#### 3.2.1 Image-Based World Model

Image-based world models generate future frames conditioned on ego actions, enabling agents to “dream” scene evolution and evaluate the consequences of different trajectories. These methods leverage modern generative models to synthesize realistic, temporally coherent videos and are typically classified into diffusion-based and autoregressive architectures.

Diffusion-Based World Models use latent video diffusion [[214](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib214), [14](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib14)] to produce multi-step rollouts. For front-view forecasting, GenAD [[296](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib296)] and Vista [[69](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib69)] incorporate temporal reasoning modules to handle complex motion patterns. Imagine-2-Drive [[71](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib71)] integrates diffusion generation into a reinforcement-learning framework, training a policy actor inside the world model. To support multi-view predictions, DriveDreamer [[265](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib265)] employs a two-stage pipeline for video synthesis and policy learning. Drive-WM [[267](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib267)] factors views within a spatiotemporal model and generates multiple plausible futures, selecting trajectories using image-based rewards.

Autoregressive (AR) Models tokenize images using VQ-VAE [[254](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib254)] and model scene evolution via next-token prediction [[59](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib59), [128](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib128), [305](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib305)]. DrivingWorld [[92](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib92)] builds a GPT-style architecture for high-fidelity long-horizon video generation. DrivingGPT [[34](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib34)] interleaves image and action tokens, unifying simulation and trajectory planning. Epona [[321](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib321)] combines AR modeling with diffusion to produce high-resolution, long-duration rollouts.

Image-based world models provide photorealistic simulations crucial for training and evaluation. However, their reliance on 2D appearance limits explicit 3D reasoning, which can hinder safety-critical long-horizon planning.

heading_path: Vision-Language-Action Models for Autonomous Driving: Past, Present, and Future
chunks.text:
#### 3.2.2 Occupancy-Based World Models

Occupancy-based world models represent the driving scene as spatiotemporal occupancy grids and predict their evolution under different actions. Instead of synthesizing raw pixels, these models focus on the geometry and semantics of free space, obstacles, and agents [[154](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib154), [171](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib171), [342](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib342)]. As shown in the middle of Figure [4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#S3.F4.1 "Figure 4 ‣ 3.2.1 Image-Based World Model ‣ 3.2 World Models for Autonomous Driving ‣ 3 Vision-Action Models ‣ Vision-Language-Action Models for Autonomous Driving: Past, Present, and Future"), AR prediction is commonly used in occupancy world models.

OccWorld [[334](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib334)] first introduces occupancy forecasting for planning, using a scene tokenizer to discretize 3D occupancy before applying a GPT-style transformer to synthesize future scenes and ego trajectories. RenderWorld [[292](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib292)] produces 3D occupancy through a self-supervised Gaussian module, while OccVAR [[112](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib112)] performs coarse-to-fine 4D occupancy forecasting. T3\text{T}^{3}Former [[282](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib282)] encodes occupancy using compact triplanes and predicts future triplane updates from multi-scale history.

T3\text{T}^{3}

An alternative line employs single-stage feedforward prediction. Drive-OccWorld [[297](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib297)] uses predicted future BEV features for action-conditioned 3D forecasting. DFIT-OccWorld [[318](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib318)] introduces a decoupled dynamic flow strategy to support efficient non-autoregressive prediction. NeMo [[96](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib96)] improves vision-based occupancy forecasting by combining it with self-supervised image reconstruction signals.

Occupancy-based models offer strong geometric fidelity and explicit free-space reasoning but rely on costly 3D annotations, which can limit scalability across diverse environments.

heading_path: Vision-Language-Action Models for Autonomous Driving: Past, Present, and Future
chunks.text:
#### 3.2.3 Latent-Based World Models

Latent-based world models bypass explicit image or occupancy forecasting and instead predict future dynamics directly in a compressed latent space. By operating on high-level features, these models capture behavioral patterns and long-horizon dependencies while avoiding the computational overhead of pixel-level generation. Regarding the forecasting strategy, the latent world model utilizes single-frame or AR prediction presented at the bottom of Figure [4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#S3.F4.1 "Figure 4 ‣ 3.2.1 Image-Based World Model ‣ 3.2 World Models for Autonomous Driving ‣ 3 Vision-Action Models ‣ Vision-Language-Action Models for Autonomous Driving: Past, Present, and Future").

Early latent models [[337](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib337), [8](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib8)] learn feature-level dynamics for planning without generating visual frames. LAW [[143](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib143)] leverages self-supervised learning to predict future scene features from current features and planned ego trajectories, enabling end-to-end driving without perception labels. World4Drive [[335](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib335)] employs vision foundation models to create latent representations from which diverse planning trajectories can be generated and evaluated. Echo-Planning [[232](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib232)] introduces a bidirectional Current→Future→Current (CFC) cycle to enforce temporal consistency in latent BEV features. For robustness in imitation learning, Covariate-Shift [[204](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib204)] addresses distribution mismatch using latent rollouts. By injecting predicted BEV features, SeerDrive [[315](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#bib.bib315)] refines both latent prediction and trajectory generation in a closed-loop manner.

Latent world models offer efficient and semantically informed forecasting. However, achieving high-quality planning still requires auxiliary supervision from 2D/3D annotations, such as bounding boxes or HD maps.

3.3 Limitations of VA Compared to VLA
chunks.text:
### 3.3 Limitations of VA Compared to VLA

While VA models remain widely deployed, they face structural limitations that hinder performance in complex, ambiguous, or long-tailed scenarios: areas where VLA models excel.

* • Limited Interpretability. VA models provide little insight into their decision-making process. In contrast, VLA models can articulate reasoning steps or explanations through language. * • Weak Generalization. VA policies lack broad world knowledge and often require environment-specific retraining. VLA models leverage large-scale pretraining to generalize better under distribution shifts and long-tailed events. * • No Chain-of-Thought Reasoning. VA models directly map pixels to actions, making it difficult to perform explicit reasoning or contextual analysis. VLAs natively support step-wise reasoning. * • No Language Understanding. VA systems cannot incorporate human instructions or high-level goals expressed in natural language. VLA models naturally integrate such inputs to guide planning and decision-making.

chunks.text:
## 4 Vision-Language-Action Models

Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models extend the Vision-Action paradigm by coupling visual perception with the multimodal reasoning capabilities of large vision-language models. Equipped with chain-of-thought style inference and broad world knowledge, these models are particularly promising for rare, ambiguous, and long-tailed driving scenarios. Table [2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4 Vision-Language-Action Models ‣ Vision-Language-Action Models for Autonomous Driving: Past, Present, and Future") summarizes typical prompting strategies, and Table [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2512.16760v2#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4 Vision-Language-Action Models ‣ Vision-Language-Action Models for Autonomous Driving: Past, Present, and Future") overviews representative VLA-based approaches.

From an architectural standpoint, current VLA methodologies for autonomous driving can be grouped into two main categories:

* • End-to-End VLA: a single model directly maps multimodal sensory inputs and language to actions. * • Dual-System VLA: a VLM provides high-level reasoning or guidance, while a specialized driving module executes fast, low-level action.

End-to-End VLA: a single model directly maps multimodal sensory inputs and language to actions.

Dual-System VLA: a VLM provides high-level reasoning or guidance, while a specialized driving module executes fast, low-level action.
